title: THE MAYORS
canon: An eleven-episode forensic documentary tracing New York City's 75-year fall through the eleven mayors who governed it, 1950 to the present — from Vincent Impellitteri's post-war heights to Zohran Mamdani's Democratic Socialist administration, told alongside one Sicilian immigrant family's parallel story. Shot cinema verite in New York City; the archive is the story, and Episode 11 films the new administration in real time. Who killed New York City? This is the report.
look: Ric Burns-homage documentary realism, forensic not hysterical: each era is rendered in its own period-correct photographic stock — 1950s newsreel black-and-white, early-Kodachrome color, pushed 1970s color negative, gritty 35mm street photography, clean present-day digital cinema. No sets for the present day: New York City IS the set. Light is always motivated by real sources visible or implied in the frame — sky, streetlamps, fire, fluorescents, press flashes — never stylized from nowhere.
note: Light Law pass 2026-07-18 — prompts from THE_MAYORS_EP01_doc-v02.fdx. Eight moment-in-time frames, all from scenes on the EP01 page (Cold Open through Act Four plus the present-day B-roll mirrors); none duplicates the old spec's six arc frames or its eleven press-history frames. No cast refs exist for anyone in EP01 (reference-manifest 2026-07-16: the only cast ref is Lindsay, who is not in this episode), so refs carry location only — the two genuine City Hall photographs, used solely where the real facade is in shot. No 2026 frame in this set: EP01 contains no scene for the sitting mayor, only narration; the standing likeness law carries forward regardless (publicSlate=false pending counsel — the 2026 mayor is never identifiable in any generated frame, per the old spec's faceless-silhouette convention). The Costello frame is faceless by the script's own order — the judge's, not counsel's.

stills.notes: COLD OPEN — '[ARCHIVAL: Lower-harbor processing photographs. A stamped ship's manifest page, names in a clerk's hand. A boy's face in a crowd, caught mid-arrival, cap pushed back.]' / 'He had a name nobody on the pier could spell. And the city took him anyway.' Why: the father's whole arrival compressed to one face at the clerk's desk — the misspelled name is the emotion, not the ship.
stills.prompt: The lower-harbor processing pier off the Battery, New York, October 1952 — a sixteen-year-old Sicilian boy stands at the clerk's high oak desk, flat cap pushed back, a rope-tied cardboard suitcase pinned between his ankles, watching upside-down as the clerk's fountain pen stalls halfway through a surname it cannot spell. The boy's face is the picture: salt-chapped, exhausted, lit with something not quite hope yet. Behind him the manifest line shuffles in wool overcoats and headscarves. The pier shed's own light does all the work — grey Atlantic daylight through high sooted windows and the open cargo doors, one bare bulb hanging over the desk, faces falling into shadow between the roof beams. Black-and-white 35mm newsreel still, heavy silver-halide grain, slight halation. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT ONE — THE CITY THAT WORKED — '[INT. — FATHER (period-evocative set, kitchen table, 1950s)]' / '(Soundbite intent... Italians were not welcome … but if you worked, nobody stopped you.)' / 'He will tell you the police were feared. He says it now almost with affection.' Why: the series' human engine is an old man remembering — the look held too long IS the interview.
stills.prompt: A documentary interview set dressed as a 1950s Lower East Side kitchen — enamel-top table, oilcloth, a bread box, a saint's calendar tacked to the wall. The father, past ninety now, sits where he sat then: thick working hands folded on the table, wedding band loose on the knuckle, eyes gone past the lens into 1952, the look held two beats too long — almost affection, almost grief. A cup of coffee untouched at his elbow. The only light is the set's own: hard daylight through the single curtained window raking one side of his face, the far side dropping into honest shadow, a warm tungsten spill from the hallway behind. Clean present-day digital cinema still, shallow focus, mixed natural color temperatures. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT TWO — THE ACCIDENTAL MAYOR — '[ARCHIVAL: O'Dwyer exiting, hat and coat.]' / 'And on September second, 1950 … O'Dwyer resigns. Officially, his health.' / 'Conveniently out of subpoena range.' Why: the founding template — power leaving without paying — carried in a downcast face that will not meet the flash. Refs hold the real City Hall portico only; distinct from the old spec's Impellitteri press scrum (different mayor, silent exit not mid-denial).
stills.prompt: The steps of New York City Hall, the morning of September 2, 1950 — Mayor William O'Dwyer leaving for the last time, hat brim pulled low, overcoat folded over one arm, eyes down and away from the three newspapermen who found him early; a single Speed Graphic flashbulb fires and he does not turn into it. His free hand grips the brass rail a beat too hard. Behind him the portico doors stand open on a dark hall. The light is what the morning gives: flat overcast September grey, even on the marble, the one flash blowing a hard white edge along his cheek and hat while everything else holds soot-toned. Black-and-white 4x5 press photograph, silver-halide grain, deep blacks. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT TWO — THE ACCIDENTAL MAYOR — '[ARCHIVAL: Vincent Impellitteri portrait. The City Council President's office, nameplate. A swearing-in, hand raised.]' / 'So on September second, 1950, by accident, Vincent Impellitteri is mayor of New York.' Why: the accidental mayor's whole story in one face — hand raised for an oath nobody planned, surprise held down by a set jaw.
stills.prompt: A plain office inside New York City Hall, September 2, 1950 — Vincent Impellitteri, a slight Sicilian-born lawyer in a dark suit, right hand raised for a swearing-in nobody planned; the city clerk holds the Bible, two aides stand where a crowd should be, and the new mayor's eyes carry the picture — a man nobody picked taking the oath anyway, jaw set against his own surprise. The desk behind him still holds papers abandoned mid-task, a Council President's nameplate not yet changed. The room's own light: tall-window daylight from one side, a green-shaded desk lamp left burning, one press flashbulb catching the raised hand hard white. Black-and-white newsreel still, fine grain, blown flash highlight, shadows left where they fall. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT THREE — MOBSTERS ON THE NEW MACHINE — '[ARCHIVAL: Frank Costello at the witness table. The famous shot … the camera locked on his HANDS only, by the judge's order, fingers twisting, a cigarette, a folded paper. His face never shown.]' Why: the script's own faceless frame — the hands confess what the face is never shown doing; the klieg light belongs to the broadcast in the room.
stills.prompt: The Foley Square federal courthouse hearing room, New York, March 1951 — the witness table of the Kefauver hearings framed exactly as the judge ordered: hands only, no face, cropped at the shoulders. Frank Costello's manicured fingers twist a folded slip of paper, a cigarette burning between two knuckles, a sweating water glass beside the microphone stand — the hands doing all the confessing the face is never shown doing. The broadcast's own klieg lights pour hard flat white across the tabletop, doubling every shadow; past the pool of light the packed room drops to darkness, a wall of grey suits in cigarette haze. Black-and-white television-era press still, harsh blown highlights on the table, coarse newsreel grain. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT THREE — MOBSTERS ON THE NEW MACHINE — 'Crowds gathered three deep at an appliance-store window watching the broadcast through the glass.' / 'That image does damage. To the mob, yes. But also to every Italian who came off a boat with nothing to do with any of it.' Why: the damage landing on one innocent face in the crowd — the moment the country's stare becomes personal.
stills.prompt: An appliance-store window on a Manhattan side street, a weekday afternoon in March 1951 — a crowd three deep pressed to the glass in hats and work jackets, watching the Kefauver hearings on a row of new television sets. In the middle of them one Italian laborer's face is quietly falling, understanding that the hands flickering on those small screens are being read as his hands; the woman beside him will not look at him. Flat midday overcast fills the street shadowless; the picture tubes throw a pale blue-grey flicker back onto the nearest faces, and the glass lays the crowd's own reflection over the broadcast. Black-and-white 35mm street photograph, deep blacks, slight window glare, honest grain. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT FOUR — THE BUILDER, AND THE FIRST DEFERRAL — '[ARCHIVAL: Cross-Bronx Expressway construction, a trench gouged through a dense residential grid. Apartment buildings standing at the lip of the cut.]' / 'the eviction of nearly four thousand families in its right-of-way alone'. Why: Moses's invoice made human — a mother and child at their window above the trench, the boxes already packed, the laundry still out.
stills.prompt: East 176th Street at the Cross-Bronx Expressway cut, the Bronx, 1952 — a tenement standing at the very lip of the trench, and in a fourth-floor kitchen window a mother holds her daughter's shoulders as both look down into the gash where the next block used to be. Behind them the room is packed into boxes, curtains already down; one line of laundry still runs from the sill because life keeps needing clean shirts. Below, steam shovels and a blasting crew work the pit. Hard noon sun drops straight into the cut, bleaching the rubble white while the trench walls and the window fall into shadow; rock dust hazes the air. Early-Kodachrome color still, saturated but dust-dulled, fine grain. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: ACT ONE — THE CITY THAT WORKED — '[B-ROLL: PRESENT DAY. The same Lower East Side blocks. A locked storefront grate... A man asleep in a doorway. A smoke-shop sign where a butcher used to be.]' / 'that is the thing that goes missing.' Why: the present-day mirror on the page — the ladder gone, told in one sleeping stranger nobody stops for. Butcher signage kept worn past reading to avoid legible-text garble.
stills.prompt: Essex Street, Lower East Side, present day, a grey weekday morning — a man asleep in the recessed doorway of a shuttered shop, curled under a sleeping bag against the rolled-down grate, one sneaker off beside him; in the next window a lit smoke-shop sign buzzes, and high on the facade the faded outline of a painted butcher's sign sits worn past reading. Sidewalk scaffolding shadows the whole block. Nobody stops. The light is only what the street gives: flat overcast daylight leaking under the scaffold boards, the smoke shop's green-white LED glow washing across the sleeping man's face, mixed and unlovely. Clean present-day digital cinema still, natural color, deep focus. No text, no watermark.
